topic: 2014-2015 FC models against the KTM SX-F
statement: The 2014-2015 Austrian-built Husqvarna FC models are the KTM SX-F of the same year with these differences: a polyamide composite subframe instead of aluminium, a left side panel that is also the airbox cover (sealed, where the KTM is vented), D.I.D DirtStar rims instead of Excel, a 20 mm rear axle on 2014 bikes (KTM 25 mm), two seat bolts hidden in the hand-holds, a handlebar switch for two ignition maps as standard, a muffler with extra sound-deadening screens, and white bodywork with its own tank and seat. From 2015 they carry Neken bars and the WP 4CS fork.

Tester findings on the 2014-2015 FC models: the sealed airbox and screened muffler choke the low-to-mid (drill holes in the left side panel, remove the backfire screen and fit a fire-retardant filter, pull the muffler screen), the rear fender cracks if the bike is lifted by it (use the hand-holds), the subframe bolt bulge catches boots, the air-filter cage is easy to seat wrong, the shift lever tip is too low stock and too high one spline up, the shock preload ring deforms, and the rear sprocket bolts and the spoke by the rim lock need checking before every ride.

topic: 2016-2018 FC models against the KTM SX-F
statement: The 2016-2018 FC models share frame, engine, geometry and suspension hardware with the KTM SX-F and differ in: a three-piece composite subframe and airbox that is nearly sealed, a Magura hydraulic clutch (KTM uses Brembo), Pro Taper bars with a slightly lower, shorter bend, a seat about 5 mm lower, D.I.D DirtStar rims, heavier GFK brake discs, a muffler with internal cones where the KTM's is straight-through (FC 450), and their own suspension settings. They weigh about 2 lb more than the KTM and feel a little softer and more forgiving in the chassis.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2018 Husqvarna FC450 race test

statement: Tester findings on the 2016-2019 FC models: the Magura clutch slave seal can fail (the KTM Brembo slave piston and seal kit fits and cures it), the airbox restricts the low-to-mid (drill the cover, or on the FC 450 also remove the muffler cones), loose spacers fall out when the seat or right side-panel bolts are removed (glue them in), the exhaust needs the shock out to remove through 2018, sprocket bolts and spokes loosen, tie-down hooks can crimp the front brake hose, and the 2017 right side panel could melt on the exhaust until a heat shield was added for 2018.

topic: 2014-2016 TC two-strokes against the KTM SX
statement: The 2014-2016 Husqvarna TC 250 and TC 125 are the KTM SX two-strokes of the same year with a polyamide composite subframe, a larger one-piece airbox cover and side panel, D.I.D DirtStar rims, a 20 mm rear axle on 2014 bikes (KTM 25 mm), two seat bolts, hand guards, their own tank (KTM shrouds do not fit) and a handlebar map switch where the KTM has a plug under the tank. Engine, carburettor and jetting are the KTM's.

A magazine test crew's 2014 TC 250 setup: fork 0.46 kg/mm springs, 370 cc oil (stock 380), compression 7 clicks out (stock 12), rebound 12 out, legs 5 mm up (flush in sand). Shock 5.4 kg/mm spring, 105 mm sag, high-speed compression 2 turns out, with a link 1.25 mm longer. Jetting (36 mm Keihin PWK): 158 main (160 in cold weather), 40 pilot (stock 42), N1EH needle on the 4th clip (N1EG in cold weather), air screw 1-1/2 turns (stock 2). Stock gearing 13/48. It makes just under 50 hp; list price about $7,200.

statement: For 2012 the 250 SX got the rising-rate linkage and a new frame in place of PDS, the swingarm from the four-strokes, a VForce3 reed block, a new airbox and boot, new fork seals and bodywork shared with the four-strokes. The engine and this chassis ran through 2016; the 2017 was all new.

The 2012-2016 250 SX makes about 50 hp on a magazine dyno, about 5 hp more than the YZ250 of the same years, and weighs 217-218 lb. It has little torque right off the bottom and snaps hard just before the midrange.

A magazine test crew's 2012 250 SX setup: fork 0.48 kg/mm springs (stock 0.44), 375 cc oil (stock 390), compression 7 clicks out (stock 12), rebound 12 out, legs 5 mm up (flush in sand). Shock 5.4 kg/mm spring (5.6 for faster or heavier riders), 105 mm sag, high-speed compression 2 turns out, low-speed 15 clicks out, rebound 12 out, with a link 1.25 mm longer than stock to stop the rear sitting high and dropping fast.

statement: The 2012 250 SX is lean as delivered. Testers went from the stock 158 main and N1EI needle to a 160 main and N1EH needle on the 3rd clip, with a 42 pilot and the air screw 1-1/2 turns out.

On the 2012-2016 250 SX one turn of the power-valve preload adjuster moves the opening point about 200 rpm within a 5,000-7,500 rpm window. KTM's accessory springs change how fast it opens: red quickest, yellow stock, green softest. There are two ignition maps: unplugging the single connector under the tank selects the soft one, which helps on hardpack.

statement: Tester findings on the 2012-2016 KTM two-strokes: the nylon shock preload ring deforms (an aluminium ring or worm-drive adjuster needs the shock apart to fit), the stock rims are soft and the spokes by the rear rim lock loosen, sprocket bolts need checking, the seat foam breaks down early, the gas-cap vent hose knots when the cap is turned (route it through a hole in the steering-stem cap), and the stock bars are low for tall riders.

The 2017 250 SX was new: an overhauled engine on the same 66.4 x 72 mm bore and stroke (new cases, ports, head and clutch), a 38 mm Mikuni TMX carburettor in place of the Keihin, the lighter frame with 20% more torsional stiffness and a wheelbase 10 mm shorter, a shock 12 mm shorter and the WP AER 48 air fork. 211 lb without fuel; list price $7,699 (2018: $7,899, with the carburettor angle changed from 12 to 7 degrees and an orange frame).

On a magazine dyno the 2018 250 SX made 47.20 hp at 8,200 rpm, with 2 hp more than the YZ250 at 6,000 rpm, 4 more at 7,000 and 1.1 more at peak, and about 3 lb-ft more torque 500 rpm lower. Against the 2014-2016 engine it gained about 5 hp in the middle and lost about 1.5 at peak. The hit is abrupt and it signs off quickly after the peak, so it wants to be short-shifted. 212 lb.

A magazine test crew's 2017-2018 250 SX setup: fork air 144 psi (stock 147; below 144 it bottoms on big hits), compression 23 clicks out, rebound 19 out, legs at the second line. Shock stock 42 N/mm spring, 107 mm sag (stock 110; 102-108 works), high-speed compression 1-1/4 turns out (stock 2), low-speed 8 clicks out (stock 15), rebound 14 out (stock 15). Gearing 14/49 in place of 14/50.

On the 2017 testers ran a 450 main with the air screw 2-1/2 turns out; on the 2018 they stayed on the 440 main with a 45 pilot. The 2018 test crew mixed fuel at 60:1 (10.7 oz of oil to 5 gallons).

Ways testers softened the 2017-2018 250 SX: the power-valve adjuster (stock is one turn in from fully out; counter-clockwise is more aggressive, clockwise smoother; move it a quarter turn at a time, and 3/4 turn was one crew's sweet spot), a 49-tooth rear sprocket, tape over the airbox vent, and unplugging the map connector under the tank for the mellow ignition curve. An aftermarket hand dial replaces the adjuster screw for about $95.

For 2012 the 125 SX and 150 SX got the rising-rate linkage and a new frame in place of PDS (about 5 lb heavier), a new swingarm, head stay and air boot, a stronger kickstarter and new suspension settings. This chassis and engine ran 2012-2015; the 2016 bikes were all new.

On a magazine dyno the 125 SX made 34.69 hp at 11,200 rpm in 2012 and 34.66 hp in 2014. It weighed 202 lb in 2012 and 206 lb in 2014. Good low-to-mid for a 125 with a softer top end than earlier KTM 125s; list price $6,499 in 2014.

statement: Tester findings on the 2016-2018 KTM two-strokes: rear spokes loosen, especially by the rim lock, and sprocket bolts need checking before every ride; the fork air bleed screw strips (10 mm T-handle on the air side; the earlier Phillips screw fits the damping side); the power-valve adjuster has a square (Robertson) socket, and a flat screwdriver works; the plastic preload ring is weak; on 2017-2018 bikes the bar mounts twist in a crash (the 2016 lower mounts with the 2017 top mount cured it) and the Mikuni carburettor is fussier than the old Keihin; the 2017 rear pads grab when hot (2016 pads); tie-down hooks can crimp the front brake hose.

The 2012-2015 150 SX is a 143.6 cc engine with a 56 x 58.4 mm bore and stroke (125 SX: 54 x 54.5 mm) and its own crank, cylinder, piston, power valve and pipe tuning. It has all-steel clutch plates with stiffer springs where the 125 uses aluminium, and 13/48 gearing against the 125's 13/50.

On a magazine dyno the 2012-2014 150 SX made 38.81-38.83 hp at 11,100 rpm, about 4 hp more than the 125 SX. It weighed 205-206.5 lb. The powerband is narrow and it only makes speed when ridden hard. List price $6,599 in 2014.

A magazine test crew's 2014 150 SX setup: fork 0.44 kg/mm springs (stock 0.42), 350 cc oil (stock 360), compression 6 clicks out (stock 12), rebound 10 out (stock 12), legs 5 mm up. Shock 4.8 kg/mm spring (heavier for riders over about 150 lb), 100 mm sag, high-speed compression 2 turns out, low-speed 15 clicks out (stock 18), rebound 15 out. Jetting (38 mm Keihin PWK): 180 main, 40 pilot, N1EJ needle on the 3rd clip, air screw 1-1/2 turns. It runs lean: listen for pinging on poor fuel, in cold air or in deep sand, and add some race fuel. Gearing 13/49 in place of 13/48, or 13/50.

statement: The 2016 150 SX was all new: an engine 4 lb lighter with a 58 x 54.5 mm bore and stroke (143.99 cc; the 125 is 54 x 54.5), a six-speed gearbox and the 125's pipe, in the lighter frame with 20% more torsional stiffness and a wheelbase 10 mm shorter, a shock 12 mm shorter and softer 4.2 N/mm fork springs. It differs from the 125 SX in cylinder, piston, power valve, head stays, ignition map and jetting. 198 lb; list price $6,899. For 2017 it got the AER air fork and a Mikuni TMX carburettor.

On a magazine dyno the 2016 150 SX made 40.60 hp at 11,500 rpm and 18.63 lb-ft; the 2017 made the same and weighed 194 lb without fuel. The power is peaky and narrow: weak at part throttle and it falls off about 500 rpm past the peak.

A magazine test crew's 2016 150 SX setup: fork 4.2 N/mm springs, compression 5 clicks out (stock 15), rebound 16 out (stock 15), legs 6 mm up. Shock 42 N/mm spring, 102 mm sag, high-speed compression 2 turns out, low-speed 6 clicks out (stock 15), rebound 9 out (stock 15). Jetting (Keihin PWK): 190 main, 52 pilot, NOZE needle on the 4th clip, air screw 3 turns out (stock 1). Gearing: 13/49 for less experienced riders, 14/49 for fast ones (stock 13/48).

statement: A magazine test crew's 2017 150 SX setup: fork air 123 psi for 155-170 lb riders and 125 psi for 170-200 lb, compression 20 clicks out (stock 15), rebound 10 out (stock 15), legs at the third line; add pressure if it dives in corners, drop it if the front pushes on entry. Shock 42 N/mm spring, 105 mm sag (110 for stability on fast tracks), high-speed compression 2 turns out, low-speed 10 clicks out (stock 15), rebound 12 out (stock 15). Jetting (Mikuni TMX 38): 460 main (stock 470), 40 pilot (stock 45), 44-74 needle on the 1st clip (stock 43-74, 3rd), air screw 3 turns out (stock 1-1/2). Power valve: adjuster fully out, then in half a turn for a wider spread. Gearing: stock 13/48; 14/49 for pros, 14/50 for tight tracks.
